runs.question: Does Insider membership help keep Gen Z customers?

calls.purpose: Compare how many Gen Z members and non-members are returning customers.
Check whether the same gap shows up in the other generations.
See how many first-time and returning Gen Z customers are members.
Count first-time and returning Gen Z customers against last year.
Split the member share of first-time Gen Z customers into stores and online.
Count first-time Gen Z customers in stores and online.
See where the sales growth from first-time Gen Z customers came from.
Check whether first-time customers of the other generations are joining less too.
Count first-time Gen Z customers who are members, against last year.
Split the member share of returning Gen Z customers into stores and online.
See where sales from returning Gen Z customers changed.
Count returning Gen Z customers in stores and online.
Check the member share of returning customers in the other generations.

answer.headline: Gen Z members are far more likely to be returning customers; sign-up among first-time Gen Z customers fell mostly online, while in stores the drop is among returning Gen Z customers.

items.text: Among Gen Z customers, {c1_member_ty} of Insider members are returning customers, against {c1_non_member_ty} of non-members.
The other generations show the same pattern: {c2_member_ty} of members against {c2_non_member_ty} of non-members.
Only {c3_first_time_ty} of first-time Gen Z customers are members, down from {c3_first_time_ly} last year, while {c3_returning_ty} of returning Gen Z customers are.
First-time Gen Z customers rose from {c4_first_time_ly} to {c4_first_time_ty}, while returning Gen Z customers fell from {c4_returning_ly} to {c4_returning_ty}.
Most first-time Gen Z customers buy in stores, {c6_store_ty} against {c6_online_ty} online, and stores added {c7_store_diff} in sales from them against {c7_online_diff} online.
In stores, the member share of first-time Gen Z customers went down from {c5_store_ly} to {c5_store_ty}; online it fell from {c5_online_ly} to {c5_online_ty}.
First-time customers of the other generations joined more than last year: the share rose from {c8_store_ly} to {c8_store_ty} in stores and from {c8_online_ly} to {c8_online_ty} online.
The number of first-time Gen Z members still rose, from {c9_ly} to {c9_ty}, as many more first-time Gen Z customers came in.
Among returning Gen Z customers, the member share fell in stores, from {c10_store_ly} to {c10_store_ty}, and rose online, from {c10_online_ly} to {c10_online_ty}.
Returning Gen Z customers in stores went down from {c12_store_ly} to {c12_store_ty}, and sales from them fell by {c11_store_diff|abs}, against {c11_online_diff} online.
For returning customers of the other generations, the member share in stores rose from {c13_store_ly} to {c13_store_ty}.
Stores are bringing in most new Gen Z customers and still sign them up at close to last year's rate; the fall in sign-up is specific to Gen Z and sits mostly online.
Membership is the strongest link to coming back that this data offers, so sign-up at the first purchase is the lever to test, starting with online checkout for Gen Z shoppers.
A fair test: show the Insider sign-up more prominently at online checkout to some first-time shoppers and not to others, then compare how many join and how many come back.
In stores, the weak spot for Gen Z is returning customers rather than first-time sign-up: fewer of them came back, and fewer of those who did are members.
For stores, try an Insider offer aimed at Gen Z customers who have bought before, in some stores and not in similar ones, and compare how many come back.
There are only {c12_store_ty} returning Gen Z customers in stores this year, so a few customers can move these shares.
The online group is small, {c6_online_ly} first-time Gen Z customers last year and {c6_online_ty} this year, so its drop rests on a handful of members.
Returning customers have had more time to join, so membership may follow loyalty rather than cause it.

Each customer appears about once in this data, so returning is read from the customer's status, not a measured repeat rate; the data also doesn't say whether the Insider flag means member at purchase or today.

runs.question: Which products are bringing in Gen Z customers right now?

calls.purpose: Count first-time Gen Z customers against last year.
Find which product families first-time Gen Z customers bought most.
Rank product families by sales growth from first-time Gen Z customers.
Find the families where Gen Z makes up the largest share of buyers.
Get the Gen Z share of all customers as a baseline.
Check how much stock the leading families have left.

answer.headline: Tabby brings in the most first-time Gen Z customers, and Tabby, Pillow Tabby and Brooklyn added the most sales from them; Tabby and Pillow Tabby are low on stock.

items.text: First-time Gen Z customers rose from {c1_ly} to {c1_ty}.
Tabby drew the most of them, {c2_tabby_ty} against {c2_tabby_ly} last year, followed by Willow ({c2_willow_ty}) and Brooklyn ({c2_brooklyn_ty}).
By sales added from first-time Gen Z customers: Tabby {c3_tabby_diff}, Pillow Tabby {c3_pillow_tabby_diff} and Brooklyn {c3_brooklyn_diff}.
Gen Z makes up {c4_mens_bag_ty} of Mens Bag buyers and {c4_pillow_tabby_ty} of Pillow Tabby buyers, against {c5_ty} across all products.
Weeks of stock left: Tabby {c6_tabby_cover} against {c6_tabby_cover_ly} last year, Pillow Tabby {c6_pillow_tabby_cover}, Brooklyn {c6_brooklyn_cover}.
Tabby and Pillow Tabby are where Gen Z acquisition and stock risk overlap, so running out could slow the flow of new Gen Z customers.
Brooklyn is growing with first-time Gen Z customers and has more stock, which makes it a candidate to feature while Tabby is short.
This shows what first-time Gen Z customers bought, not what brought them in; there is no traffic or campaign data.
Most families have only a few dozen first-time Gen Z customers, so a handful of orders can change the ranking, and Mens Bag is a small family.

runs.question: Which age group spends more per order?

calls.purpose: Compare average order value across age groups, this year and last.
Check whether the gaps between age groups are larger than normal variation.
Get the average order value of all customers as a baseline.
Compare full-price stores with outlets, to see how much the store type matters.
Split Gen Z orders into first-time and returning customers.

answer.headline: Gen Z spends the most per order, but only slightly more than Millennials; whether the order is at a full-price store or an outlet makes a much bigger difference.

items.text: Average order value is {c1_gen_z_ty} for Gen Z, {c1_millennial_ty} for Millennials, {c1_boomer_ty} for Boomers and {c1_gen_x_ty} for Gen X, against {c3_ty} for all customers.
The likely range is {c2_gen_z_low} to {c2_gen_z_high} for Gen Z and {c2_millennial_low} to {c2_millennial_high} for Millennials, so the two overlap.
Gen Z's average order is close to last year's {c1_gen_z_ly}, while Millennials' rose from {c1_millennial_ly} to {c1_millennial_ty}.
Orders at full-price stores average {c4_full_price_ty}, against {c4_outlet_ty} at outlets.
Within Gen Z, first-time customers spend {c5_first_time_ty} per order and returning customers {c5_returning_ty}, down from {c5_returning_ly} last year.
Age group on its own is a weak guide to order value; store type, and whether it is a customer's first purchase, explain more of the difference.
Each order in this data is a single line with about one item, so order value mostly reflects the price of the item bought.
Order value is after discounts, and the data has no discount or margin detail.
